articles.title_orig: US Closes Loophole That Allowed China To Remotely Access Nvidia Chips
articles.title_zh: US Closes Loophole That Allowed China To Remotely Access Nvidia Chips
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China .
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council."
The rule came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center the Nvidia scandal, on the so-called entity list, which would restrict certain exports to it.
Share prices of Nvidia and other companies linked to artificial intelligence trade fell after the interim rule was announced, among them the chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices .
"The Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," the IFR issued Monday says.
"These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models," the rule said.
The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

articles.title_orig: Trump says he may meet with Kim Jong Un while in China for APEC as US looks to reengage North Korea on nuclear program
articles.title_zh: Trump says he may meet with Kim Jong Un while in China for APEC as US looks to reengage North Korea on nuclear program
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.title_zh: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government.
The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the trial , saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions.
A lawyer for several of the defendants, speaking on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients.
When asked about those claims, the Bahraini government said in a statement that all of the defendants had been “afforded their full legal rights and safeguards, including the right of defense,” and that complaints of mistreatment would be referred for investigation.
“This case was about criminal conduct, not faith or belief,” the government added.
The Bahraini authorities had accused the defendants of forming a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. According to a statement from the Bahraini public prosecution department, published by the state news agency, the defendants had worked to undermine the Bahraini government, and the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials.
“They had also sought to change the system of government by force and unlawful means through incitement to commit terrorist acts, acts of rioting and sabotage,” the statement added.

articles.title_orig: Will OpenAI and Anthropic benefit from China chip restrictions
articles.title_zh: Will OpenAI and Anthropic benefit from China chip restrictions
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
In the Loop Host Ejaaz Ahamadeen takes a closer look at former Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang affair timeline and identifies who may benefit most.
That leads me to the third bit of evidence, which is Anthropic and Open AI are reportedly bonding and forming an alliance to push forward a regulation or law to impose a ban on chip exports to China.
Now, the initial and obvious reaction to this is, huh, that's probably good, right?
Like if we ban them from getting access to our chips, they won't be able to build breaking edge AI and we will end up winning the race.
And certainly, there is an argument for this, but it seems pretty coincidental that they're accelerating this right when the key advocate for open source and selling chips to anyone and everyone, not just China, is hurting.
And make no mistake, the outcome from this would be there's an increasing concentration risk being placed in America itself.
And guess who the two biggest labs are that are buying these chips?
It's Anthropic and Open AI, so it would disproportionately benefit them.
Less competition out there. Remember, Chinese AI labs were the biggest advocates for open models, and a lot of American companies and founders actually use Chinese models.
So I can assume they're looking at this and thinking no one wins either way.
And the last thing I'll say is, if Alice Huang was actually a Chinese spy, she did an absolutely terrible job of doing it.
She made no effort to try and hide the fact she was flying to China every other week.
She was being close to Jensen Huang in public. She wasn't exactly trying to hide it.
She was posting social media photos on WeChat, which is the Chinese public social media site, of her and Jensen Huang flexing.
She was publicly attending investing meetings with Chinese AI labs to be like, hey, can I invest?
And the idea here is, if she ended up not being a Chinese spy, that wouldn't surprise me.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty after release from secure hospital
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty after release from secure hospital
articles.content_orig:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.
21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj breached Rockstar Games in 2022 whilst he was on bail for multiple other hacking offences and under police protection.
He was being housed in a Travelodge in Bicester to protect him from rival hackers who threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to cooperate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.79m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
At the time, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand in a traditional trial due to the severity of his autism, so instead he was given what is known as a trial of the facts.
The jury was asked to determine whether or not he committed the alleged acts - not if he did so with criminal intent.
In December 2023 the court ruled that he would remain at a secure hospital for life unless doctors deem him no longer a danger.
A routine assessment late last year deemed that he was now fit to stand a criminal trial which was scheduled to take place at Woolwhich Crown Court.
But Kurtaj pleaded guilty to all offences.
He sat in the dock with short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt but no tie.
The now 21-year-old blinked frequently during the hearing and stood to confirm his name, and pled guilty to all counts with no visible emotion.
Those included hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber where he used social engineering techniques to gain access to internal systems.
The court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.
His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.
Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.
The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 from individual victims.
Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers whilst in custody including multiple biting incidents.
Whilst in prison he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.
Kurtaj will be sentenced at a later date.
In the 2023 original trial, another Lapsus$ member, who was 17, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.
The 17-year-old, who could not be named at the time due to his age, was sentenced to an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order, including intense supervision and a ban on using VPNs online.
Earlier this year that same hacker, now named as Thalha Jubair, was jailed for five years and six months after continuing his cyber crime offences with another group known as Scattered Spider.
Amongst victims was Transport for London which was subjected to a disruptive cyber attack that caused around £39m of damage and caused chaos inside the firm.

articles.title_orig: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
articles.title_zh: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
articles.content_orig:
Filipino-US journalist Maria Ressa’s new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy – and how we can fight back
Maria Ressa keeps apologising. “Sorry, I’m hyper, too much coffee!” she says at one point. “Sorry, I can rant for a long time, so you have to stop me!” she says at another.
Ressa can be forgiven for firing on all cylinders. The Nobel peace prize laureate has just been to a screening in Britain of The Social Reckoning, which offers an unflattering portrayal of the tech titan Mark Zuckerberg, a man she regards as a “dictator”. Now she is speaking to the Guardian at a hotel in Washington’s Dupont Circle a few days before Americans vote in critical midterm elections.
Ressa, a 63-year-old, 5ft 2in force of nature, reflects: “I feel like the train is coming at us in slow motion and we’re standing on the train tracks.”
The Filipino and American journalist has been sounding alarms for a decade . In 2016 she warned Zuckerberg and other Silicon Valley executives that an authoritarian disinformation model being tested in the Philippines would soon be exported to the west. Like Cassandra, she was not believed. Now, with Donald Trump in the White House and tech billionaires actively reshaping the US state, Ressa has a new cri de cœur.
The Fight Back : A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators is a survival manual for confronting the convergence of authoritarian governance and tech oligarchy. It finds democracies facing a crisis of truth (the breakdown of facts and shared reality), a crisis of order (the breakdown of law and international rules) and a crisis of accountability (institutions are captured, the law is weaponised and the most powerful economic and tech actors operate without democratic oversight).
Ressa’s warnings are rooted in experience. She spent nearly two decades as an investigative reporter and bureau chief for CNN in Manila and Jakarta, covering terrorism, ethnic conflict and the precarious transitions of post-authoritarian societies across south-east Asia.
In 2012, convinced that digital technology offered a tool to empower citizens and demand transparency, she co-founded Rappler , an independent, digital-first news organisation in the Philippines. Blending hard-nosed investigative journalism with data science and community engagement, Rappler quickly established itself as a vital watchdog in a fragile democracy.
When Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 , Ressa found herself at the front line of a terrifying global experiment. As Duterte unleashed a bloody extrajudicial drug war that claimed thousands of lives, his regime weaponised social media to silence critics, deploying state-backed troll armies to poison public discourse and wage psychological warfare.
Rappler’s reporting exposed the machinery of manufactured outrage, making Ressa the authoritarian government’s public enemy number one. She endured an onslaught of online harassment, including rape threats and death threats, and an aggressive legal offensive by the state, with 11 cases filed against her, including charges of cyber libel and tax evasion.
Rather than flee or capitulate, she posted bail 10 times and turned her courtroom battles into an international campaign for press freedom. In 2021 she was awarded the Nobel peace prize , alongside Russian journalist Dmitry Muratov, for safeguarding the freedom of expression that underpins democracy.
The personal toll has been immense. “I wish I could get more sleep,” she says matter-of-factly. “I worked in war zones and the only difference is you’d walk into conflict and stay two weeks to a month and then you could come out and decompress for a month. This is a decade of non-decompression.”
Ressa’s experience in the Philippines informs The Fight Back, but she argues that the threat is now much wider. A report published earlier this year by the V-Dem Institute, a Swedish research centre that measures the health of democracies worldwide, found that democracy had fallen back to 1978 levels for the average global citizen, with three-quarters of the world’s population living under autocratic rule.
In the US, the level of democracy had fallen to its lowest point since 1965. The report contained a sentence that Ressa had to read three times and still haunts her: “The speed with which American democracy is currently dismantled is unprecedented in modern history.”
Early in Trump’s second term, comparisons with authoritarian leaders such as Duterte in the Philippines and Viktor Orbán in Hungary were commonplace. But it soon became apparent that the US president was moving with a scope and speed that would leave even those autocrats envious.
Ressa writes: “What took Hungary’s Orbán four years, Serbia’s Vučić eight years, India’s Modi and Turkey’s Erdoğan a decade, Trump accomplished in one year. Legislative constraints lost one-third of their value in 2025, the lowest in more than one hundred years. As in the Philippines, Congress has effectively abdicated its oversight role. At least 55% of the 320 objectives set out by the far-­right Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 have already been achieved.”
The rise of technology has become a driving force behind democratic decay. Ressa writes: “There are two dictators in my story: Duterte and Zuckerberg. This is not hyperbole. This is a statement about power, accountability – and impunity – in the 21st century.”
The fusion of state power and oligarchy was symbolised on 20 January 2025, inauguration day , when tech leaders including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, Sergey Brin, Tim Cook and Sam Altman were given prominent seats ahead of Trump’s cabinet nominees as he took the oath of office.
The symbiotic relationship operates through mutual self-interest: autocrats require tech platforms to distribute propaganda and paralyse public opposition, while tech oligarchs require state deregulation, tax relief, military contracts, and protection from international antitrust enforcement.
Which poses the bigger threat, Trump or big tech? Ressa has no hesitation in answering: “The big tech, because they themselves, the CEOs, are now saying: stop us. That’s kind of performative. You can stop yourself! You’re the one building this.”
Even Rappler was built as a digital-first newsroom that partnered with platforms and engineered tech. Wielding her phone, Ressa acknowledges: “We’re frenemies. I like tech. Rappler is a partner of every tech company. We build tech.”
But when she begged tech companies to “prioritise facts”, she realised facts have never been part of the AI equation. “It’s a probabilistic machine, which actually discounts facts. When you put that as the operating system of public information you create what we’re living through now. Then they made it worse because they added algorithms that will keep you scrolling longer so that means fear, anger, hate. It is the worst of who we are.”
She regards big tech as predatory and extractive. Their monopolies built valuations by ingesting journalism without compensation. “The raw material is the world’s knowledge. It is what we write that is expensive. They just scrape it.”
And by engineering algorithms for sensationalism and “outrage machine”, platforms altered human psychology, Ressa argues. “The incentive structure of our world changed with big tech. I always say to my friends who have kids: imagine if you keep telling your child, ‘Lie. I’m going to keep rewarding you, and then keep lying and I’m going to keep rewarding you.’ What kind of adult does your child become? That’s the world we’re creating.”
The new generation of tech overlords are, in her view, dictators. “They make decisions for us without our inputs, without any accountability, and it impacts all of us. This is a public safety issue. It’s like taking the lead out of your water. Every day that governments do not regulate, they lose more and more of their power.”
No figure illustrates this surrender more starkly than Elon

articles.title_orig: Sony 27-Inch Gaming Monitor With DualSense Charging Hook Review: A Piece Of PC History
articles.title_zh: Sony 27-Inch Gaming Monitor With DualSense Charging Hook Review: A Piece Of PC History
articles.content_orig:
It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.
It's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it. News broke in March that Sony would no longer bring its first-party games to PC, reversing course after a six-year run on desktops and teeing up a summer of heartbreak in the video game world. On the heels of this decision, Sony debuted the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook, advertising it as a desktop-geared peripheral that's compatible with PC, PS5 and a lineup of PlayStation accessories. It's sleek, it's sturdy, it has a crisp QHD display that supports VRR and HDR, and it features a buttery screen that handles glare well.
At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory. But more than anything, it feels like a vestigial remnant of Sony's abandoned plans to infiltrate the PC space.
The DualSense monitor has a 27-inch IPS display with QHD (2,560 x 1,440 pixels) resolution and a 240Hz refresh rate that supports VRR. Here we have the first sign that this thing was originally designed for PC play: The PS5 and PS5 Pro max out at 120Hz, and the monitor's 240Hz cap was included with PC play in mind.
It supports HDR on the spec sheet, but with a peak brightness of 350 nits and no advanced local dimming, you're mostly getting a broader range of colors rather than the eye-popping highlights the term might suggest. There's also a stereo speaker built into the display, and while its output is slightly tinny and lacking bass as you'd expect, it's perfectly acceptable. Put simply, this is a pretty standard gaming monitor in 2026.
As far as inputs go, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, two USB-A slots, one USB-C connection and a 3.5mm audio output. They're tucked into a divot on the rear of the monitor and pointed downward, with a clever cable management hook that can be popped out from the stand's neck, keeping things as organized as possible.
The monitor is compatible with PC, Mac, PS5 and PS5 Pro, plus it can hold and charge a DualSense or DualSense Edge gamepad. It also functions with the PlayStation Link adapter, which enables Sony's Pulse and Pulse Elite wireless headsets, Pulse Explore earbuds and Pulse Elevate wireless speakers (at least theoretically). The Pulse headset will hit the market this month, while the Elevate speakers were just recently delayed indefinitely, extending the last echoes of a grander desktop scheme.
The DualSense charging dock swings down from behind the screen and hangs below the frame, and it's actually the star of the show. It's truly cute and also incredibly useful. Having a dedicated, out-of-the-way spot to store and charge an often-used gamepad is clutch.
The DualSense monitor is a noticeable upgrade from both the 27-inch Samsung 1440p/144Hz TN display and the 24-inch Alienware 1080p/240Hz IPS display that I currently use. This improvement applies not only to gaming scenarios, but also your standard PC use cases, like working, creating, watching YouTube, scrolling Reddit and streaming Real Housewives .
Sony's marketing positions the monitor as a display for your desktop PS5, but this is an uncommon console configuration and it's one that I don't personally have set up in my home. So, I tested out the monitor the way most players will use it, as a PC peripheral that happens to hold and charge my spare DualSense. This worked out exceedingly well for my gaming habits, considering I play Overwatch on PC and PS5, and I prefer to use a DualSense for both (keyboard and mouse players, don't come for me). However, outside of this one title, I tend to use the Wolverine V3 Pro for my Steam games, and there's no place to adorably dangle any non-DualSense gamepad from Sony's latest display. This is also true for literally every other monitor, of course.
I plugged in a set of Creative Pebble speakers and my PC, popped my favorite DualSense Edge on the dock, clipped a Logitech camera and Elgato light to the top of the monitor, and I was good to go. The display naturally rests parallel to the stand neck and it can be tilted upward about 30 degrees, but not downward. The tilt action is fluid and it sticks in place well. Shifting the screen vertically is less enjoyable but still easy: Hold a button at the back of the neck and the monitor clicks into place at varying levels. If you want to lower it more than 21mm from the top, you have to hide the charging dock first.
There's a large sliding glass door beside my desk, providing ample opportunity to test the monitor's glare-management abilities. The DualSense display has an eggshell-like coating that eats light like it's late for dinner, and it maintains a bright, crisp image even in a sun-drenched room. Things only improve in dimmer conditions, and the monitor's 240Hz refresh rate is a dream compared with my previous cap of 144Hz. With 1440p resolution, VRR and up to 240 fps in-game, I don't find myself longing for 4K visuals while playing Overwatch or any other game. Of course, I'm not coming from a 4K monitor, so I would say that.
The monitor also looks great on the desk, with a wide and thin metal base, sleek cylindrical stand neck and subtle branding. Maybe my previous display was just severely unstable, but I find the DualSense monitor to be surprisingly sturdy, especially considering its minimal design. Say you share a desk with someone who has a habit of idly bouncing their legs throughout the day, intermittently shaking the entire workspace and sometimes even knocking over your aesthetically placed Sanrio figurines. (A totally random, hypothetical example, of course). The Sony Gaming Monitor holds up well to this type of abuse, wobbling just slightly even under extreme leg-bouncing conditions. It's far more stable than my previous monitor, and it doesn't make plastic creaking noises when it does sway. All told, it's a sturdy piece of equipment.
Sony's 2026 PlayStation-branded gaming monitor is sleek, clever and cute, and at $349, it's a solid investment for anyone who even occasionally uses a PlayStation controller at the desk. My final read on the dock is that it's dope: It charges and stores the DualSense in a cool way, and provides a function that no other monitor will have. Even if you don't ever pull the charging dock down, this is a capable and clean display.
Sony clearly started building the 27-inch DualSense monitor before reversing its plans to take over the PC space, so in many ways, this peripheral exists as a physical reminder of a future that will never be. You could say it's already a piece of gaming history, something that feels more ephemeral by the day .

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Store App Receives A Small But Worthwhile Update, Here Are The Patch Notes
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Store App Receives A Small But Worthwhile Update, Here Are The Patch Notes
articles.content_orig:
Remember the dedicated Nintendo Store mobile app? Honestly, we sometimes forget about it too. But hey, Nintendo is still updating it, and the latest patch should make it a little easier to see what you have been up to on your Switch this year.
The ver. 3.4.0 update launched on iOS and Android earlier today, and it seems to be all about making the user experience that bit better.
The big change this time around is that you can now find information about your DLC and other software habits on the Play Activity screen, but there have also been some tweaks to the User Page and more.
Far from anything groundbreaking, then, but a worthwhile little addition to anyone wanting some more info from their Play Activity rundown.
You'll find the (admittedly, very short) patch notes from the App Store below:
・ Information about downloadable content and other types of software can now be found on the play activity screen. ・ Design changes have been made to improve the readability of the user page. ・ Various improvements and fixes have been made.
Do we wish that all of these disparate Nintendo apps were combined into one? Sure! Are we pleased to see Nintendo is still working to improve them behind the scenes? Absolutely.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia set to deliver first life-after-Huang briefing
articles.title_zh: Nvidia set to deliver first life-after-Huang briefing
articles.content_orig:
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week.
"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ).
Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.
"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.
Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."
The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.
CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.
Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.
Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.
AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.
Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.
"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."
The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.
Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.
"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

articles.title_orig: Is Jensen Huang Plotting a Comeback?
articles.title_zh: Is Jensen Huang Plotting a Comeback?
articles.content_orig:
Andrew here. The Jensen Huang –Nvidia tale has escalated into a high-stakes tug of war.
On one side, Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures are mounting a pressure campaign to reinstate Huang as C.E.O. But Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a “dramatic shake-up” and an outside replacement, citing concerns that Nvidia may have bypassed export laws by selling chips to Chinese-linked intermediaries. (Adding a new wrinkle, Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang , the Chinese executive at the center of the scandal, left the firm in August 2025.)
What happens next is anyone’s guess. The former Nvidia chief is expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks. But the ultimate showdown may happen overseas: President Trump is heading to China to meet President Xi Jinping , where this topic is almost certain to come up. Or is it? More below.
It’s been four days since Jensen Huang resigned as the C.E.O. of Nvidia, after news reports said he had an affair with Alice Huang , the data center executive U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy. (He also had an affair with a direct subordinate, The Times has reported.)
Now, some of Silicon Valley’s biggest heavyweights want to reinstate Huang, even as some Trump administration officials called for new blood atop the chip maker at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.
Yet there are signs that President Trump himself may not raise the issue even as he prepares to meet with Xi Jinping , China’s top leader.
Huang is reportedly on board with efforts to bring him back, The Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources. Ever since he resigned, many in Silicon Valley have wondered whether he would lead a comeback, much as Sam Altman did after briefly being ousted from OpenAI nearly three years ago.

articles.title_orig: Former SEC chair Gary Gensler warns AI bubble is likely to cause recession before 2028 election
articles.title_zh: Former SEC chair Gary Gensler warns AI bubble is likely to cause recession before 2028 election
articles.content_orig:
The former SEC chair told CNN he expects a downturn as significant as the dot-com crash, with bankruptcies among neocloud firms
Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler told CNN that the AI boom is a bubble likely to burst and drag the economy into recession ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
"It's already a bubble," Gensler said, according to CNN. He led the SEC from 2021 until 2025 and is now a professor at MIT.
Gensler pointed to the money flowing into AI infrastructure, which totals $800 billion a year by some estimates, according to CNN. "The Big Tech companies are spending five times more in 2026 than they were just three years ago," he said.
“History tells us that when you have a new technology and a significant investment ... you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” Gensler said. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.” He cited railroads, 1920s electricity and the 1990s internet as earlier technologies that suffered steep declines once their infrastructure had been built on expectations of future revenue.
He also raised concerns about how the spending is financed, pointing to circular deals and intricate off-balance-sheet structures that make the true scale of exposure hard to see. "I think history will show that they loaned too much money, too fast," he said.
Gensler named neoclouds, which lease supercomputing capacity to AI developers, as the likely first casualties. "The major companies will survive. It's these neocloud companies where we're going to see some breakage and bankruptcies," he said.
He said he expects the downturn to rival the dot-com bust of the early 2000s in significance, though not to reach the severity of the subprime housing collapse that triggered the 2008 financial crisis. "I think we're going to have this repricing and a softening of the economy that happens before November 2028," he said, according to CNN. "I can't say exactly when and how stormy, but I would be battening down some hatches."
Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, called Gensler's scenario "plausible" but disagreed that a burst is coming, according to CNN. "It's a self-correcting bubble," Yardeni said, adding that chipmakers now trade at lower price-to-earnings multiples than the market overall. "There is no irrational exuberance in valuations," he said.
The warning comes days after Nvidia $NVDA said CEO Jensen Huang had resigned with immediate effect . Nvidia has committed roughly $10 billion to a private placement of Anthropic stock that is set to close alongside Anthropic's IPO.
Anthropic plans to price its IPO on Nov. 18 . Combined with the private placement, the offering would bring in $90.4 billion if it lands at the top of the marketed range. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market on Nov. 19 under the symbol ANT.

articles.title_orig: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.title_zh: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as ‘role models’ on surprise Ukraine visit
articles.title_zh: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as ‘role models’ on surprise Ukraine visit
articles.content_orig:
By OLIVIA DAY, ASSISTANT NEWS EDITOR, AUSTRALIA
Published: 17:00 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 02:52 EST, 16 November 2026
The Duke of Sussex met with wounded veterans and medics during a surprise visit to Ukraine over the weekend, telling them: 'You're going to win the war.'
Prince Harry's arrival in the western city of Lviv on Saturday marked his fourth visit to the country since the start of the conflict with Russia.
The 42-year-old visited the Superhumans Centre - a specialised medical, prosthetics, and rehabilitation facility in the city and took the stage at the first international War Trauma Conference at the All-Ukrainian War Trauma Center.
Although he acknowledged he had 'taken a risk to come here', Harry told the crowd: 'Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth.
'You're going to win the war and then you're going to be set up for success.'
Harry said Ukraine's experience in helping injured military personnel and civilians will become the foundation for rebuilding the country after the war.
The War Trauma Conference is the first to be dedicated to modern approaches for treating and rehabilitating people suffering from combat-related trauma.
Harry was dressed casually in a dark, hooded, puffer jacket, dark blue trousers and brown desert boots as he attended a series of events.
The Duke of Sussex has met with wounded veterans and medics during a surprise visit to Ukraine, telling them: 'You're going to win the war'
He was later seen posing with organisers of Ukraine's Invictus Games. He is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games and the Invictus Games Foundation
Harry (pictured holding up a child in Lliv) said he felt 'welcome' and 'warmth' every time he visited Ukraine. His most recent over the weekend is the fourth since the conflict began
In a school sports hall, the Duke (pictured) watched wheelchair rugby players as they vied for a place in Ukraine's team at next year's Invictus Games
He was pictured grinning ear-to-ear as he held up a little boy for a photo and when he posed with organisers of Ukraine's Invictus Games.
In a school sports hall, he watched wheelchair rugby players as they vied for a place in Ukraine's team at next year's Invictus Games and joined in for a game of pickleball.
Ukraine is planning to send 60 competitors – its largest ever team – to the 2027 edition of the event, which is scheduled to take place in Birmingham.
The country has about 1.4million combat veterans, more than 10 per cent of whom have disabilities.
Later on Saturday, Harry told wounded veterans joining the Invictus movement : 'When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games.'
At the rugby game, he hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, a former contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025, who has an amputated leg.
The 41-year-old with a large tattoo on one arm and deep smile lines, explained to the duke that he is 'still an active serviceman'.

'So when do you find time to train?' Harry asked in surprise.
Mr Odainyk said afterwards he told the duke that his involvement in such sport 'all started and continues with the Invictus Games'.
The duke's last visit to Ukraine was in April 2026, just days after he finished a pseudo-royal tour of Australia with his wife Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex .
Harry told reporters during the trip that he was 'not here as a politician' but as 'a soldier who understands service' and a 'humanitarian'.
He urged Vladimir Putin to 'stop this war' with Ukraine and accused the Russians of carrying out 'mass killings and torture '.
In September 2025, the duke made his second visit to Ukraine and his first to Kyiv. The city had been hit with Russian cruise missiles just two days earlier.
During that visit, he declared he will do 'everything possible' to help Ukrainian soldiers and service personnel injured in the three-year war with Russia.
In April 2025, Harry met with war victims in his first trip to Ukraine, this time to Lviv.
The visit to the area in western Ukraine, that has frequently been targeted with Russian missiles, was not announced until after Harry was out of the country.
Harry, 42, is the second member of the royal family to visit Ukraine. His aunt, Sophie, the Duchess of Edinburgh, became the first British royal to travel to the country since Russia's 2022 invasion when she made an unannounced visit to Kyiv in 2024 .

articles.title_orig: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.title_zh: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.content_orig:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

articles.title_orig: Morning Bid: AI selloff resumes as Nvidia earnings loom
articles.title_zh: Morning Bid: AI selloff resumes as Nvidia earnings loom
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders awaited a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic this week.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.6%, while the S&P 500 fell 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 186 points, or 0.4%.
Shares in Nvidia were down more than 1%. On Monday, the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent the chipmaker's computing power located in other countries. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend called for a " dramatic shakeup " at Nvidia, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
The embattled chipmaker is preparing to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as chief executive.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices lost 6%, 5% and 4%, respectively. Memory chip name Sandisk pulled back about 7%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined more than 5%, while software stock Oracle moved down nearly 3%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering . The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
The three major averages kicked off the first trading session of the week in the red.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 declined 0.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 78 points, or 0.2%.
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China .
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." Read more .
Factory activity eased in  New York State during November though employment expanded at the fastest pace in more than four years, the regional Federal Reserve reported Monday.
The New York Fed's Empire State Manufacturing Index posted a reading of 7.8, down 18 points from October and below the Dow Jones consensus for 16.7. The index measures the difference between companies reporting growth against contraction, so a positive number still represents expansion.
Much of the decline came in new orders, which fell 20.2 points to 3.0. However, the employment index jumped to 18.1, growth of 7.8 points and its highest since June 2022. Prices also continued to climb but at a slower pace as the prices paid index fell 14 points to 45.9.
Nvidia continues to lose its luster, with two more Wall Street analysts lowering their price targets on the stock following a scandal that led to Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO.
Mizuho, which has an outperform on the chipmaker, lowered its price target on shares to $220 from $250. That still suggests 35% upside from Friday's close. UBS has a buy rating on the stock. It revised its price target on shares down to $240 from $300, which is 47% above the level at which Nvidia last closed.
"We believe ex-CEO Jensen was viewed as the global dealmaker 'AI banker', and key innovator," Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh said in a note to clients. "The significant NVDA ~32% stock decline from the Oct peak (vs. the SOX down 23%), reflects the 'Jensen/founder' premium lost. We believe the CEO departure also adds a 6-7-month management overhang, as [the] company comes under the US gov't microscope."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Check out CNBC's live blog here for more on the stocks making premarket moves.
— Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert
UniCredit 's takeover of Commerzbank has been given the go-ahead by European competition regulators.
The European Commission on Monday gave antitrust approval to the Italian lender's bid to take control of its German peer, following similar consent from the European Central Bank last month.
That now clears the path for the takeover, with UniCredit's integration plan expected to begin early next year.
"Our approval of UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank shows that it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's first executive vice-president for a clean, just and competitive transition.
Shares in Milan-listed UniCredit were 0.62% lower in morning trade. Commerzbank was down 1% in Frankfurt.
Nvidia 's stock fell 1.72% in premarket trading, continuing its slide after losing hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.
Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
Oil prices moved higher on Monday, with Brent crude — the global price benchmark — rising 0.30% to $96.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures added 0.49% to $89.03.
The rise comes after two oil tankers reportedly struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, which cited Iran's Revolutionary Guard. It followed similar reported incidents on Sunday and Monday.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was almost 0.1% higher in early dealmaking, as most continental sectors made gains and major bourses were mixed shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.).
Healthcare stocks advanced 0.79%, followed by telecommunications, which were up 0.67%, as household goods gained 0.63%. Basic resources shed 1.67%
Among regional bourses, the French CAC 40 led early gains, rising 0.30%, while the U.K. FTSE 100 added 0.22%. Germany's DAX fell 0.10%, and the Italian FTSE MIB was 0.39% down.
European stock markets are expected to start the new trading week in mostly negative territory.
Stoxx 50 futures seen opening almost 0.1% lower, with all of the continent's major bourses in the red.
The French CAC 40 was almost 0.2% down ahead of Monday's session, while the Italian FTSE MIB was about 0.1% lower.
Futures tied to the U.K. FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX were seen opening around the flatline.
Asian tech heavyweights slid on Monday as investors continued to grapple with the fallout from developments at chip giant Nvidia, with former CEO Jensen Huang reportedly mulling a dramatic comeback.
Key Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company all plunged, with SK Hynix down over 5.6%. Samsung and TSMC lost about 3% each.

articles.title_orig: Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise
articles.title_zh: Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise
articles.content_orig:
This holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.
"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.
Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.
"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year."
The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.
According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.
Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.
At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.
Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.
And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.
Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail , which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's .
"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said.
Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?
It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.
UPS CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers."
Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.
"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.
Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company's annual forecast . Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.
"The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers said. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf."
ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.
It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding new team members.
"Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania said.
Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.
A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry."
Amit Regev, CEO of drone company Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.
"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev said.
Retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.
Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.
"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev said. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones."

articles.title_orig: Cantwell Accuses Commerce Department of Letting AI Chips Reach China as Xi Meeting Nears
articles.title_zh: Cantwell Accuses Commerce Department of Letting AI Chips Reach China as Xi Meeting Nears
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.
