articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Controversy Could Backfire on China, Chamath Palihapitiya Says — Washington May Get
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Controversy Could Backfire on China, Chamath Palihapitiya Says — Washington May Get
articles.content_orig:
By ELIOT FORCE, US NEWS REPORTER
Published: 15:17 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 02:54 EST, 16 November 2026
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is vying to reclaim the position he resigned from just days ago after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, according to a report.
Huang, 63, stepped down on Thursday from the top role at the $4 trillion tech giant he co-founded after it was revealed that he may have also had a second affair with Nvidia's Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell.
Hours later, Reuters reported that the former CEO had yet another, third extramarital relationship with another unidentified Nvidia employee. Huang has only admitted to the affair with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, whom he is not related to.
Despite the seriousness and recency of the philandering accusations, Huang has already been holding discussions with powerful Silicon Valley figures about returning as CEO, sources involved in the effort told the Financial Times .
An ally of the ex-CEO told the publication that Silicon Valley executives have been putting together a 'war room' to lobby for Huang's return to Nvidia.
The executives are hoping to gain backing from the White House , and their efforts are being supported by Huang behind the scenes, the source said.
Many investors, Nvidia employees and Silicon Valley executives have also already publicly supported Huang, citing his enormously successful 33-year leadership of the company and vision that placed the business at the heart of the AI boom.
An open letter calling for Huang's return has been supported by Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as nearly 9,000 former and current Nvidia employees and more than 83,000 investors.
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is plotting a return to the position he stepped down from just days ago, according to sources involved in the effort. He is pictured with his wife, Lori
Huang has admitted to having an affair with businesswoman Alice Huang (left), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy
Huang has also been accused of having an affair with Nvidia's Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell (right) and another unidentified Nvidia employee
Although the executives backing Huang are hoping to enlist the White House's help, they may run into resistance, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a 'dramatic shakeup' in leadership at Nvidia.
President Trump has maintained a positive tone about Huang since the affairs were reported and the ex-CEO stepped down, calling him 'a tremendous talent.'
Trump also said, however, that Huang was right to resign if it is confirmed that Alice was a spy.
'It's sad. He’s a tremendous talent. He did something nobody else did. He has a chip that’s so complex, so brilliant, you can’t copy it. What he’s done is incredible, he built an incredible company,' Trump told CNN's Stephen A Smith on Thursday.
Smith asked Trump point blank if Huang was right to step down, which led to a rare pause from Trump before answering.
'The big thing was, was the woman a spy? If the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy perhaps it would be different,' the president said.
Alice is an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect has smuggled restricted Nvidia chips to China.
Authorities also believe Alice was tasked with obtaining sensitive information from Huang and influencing Nvidia's business decisions to enhance the Chinese market's access to the company's chips.
Huang's potential return is being backed by Silicon Valley executives in public and behind the scenes, according to sources involved in the effort
Huang's supporters are vying for his return despite the admitted affair with Alice due to the ex-CEO's successful 33-year leadership of the company
Nvidia has strict rules on relationships between colleagues, which could make Huang's return particularly challenging. He is pictured with his wife
Powell, the Nvidia executive Huang is accused of having a second affair with, is married like Huang, and Nvidia has strict rules on relationships between colleagues, particularly bosses and employees.
That could make the ex-CEO's hopes of returning to the company particularly challenging, as 'having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence,' a source involved in the reinstatement efforts admitted to the Financial Times.
Huang did not have a controlling share of Nvidia in contrast to many other Silicon Valley executives, which made him unable to override any board decision.
The board is now being headed by interim CEO Colette Kress, who previously held the title of Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.
Nvidia's market cap has dropped 12.75 percent since Huang's affair disclosure and resignation, and it has plunged around 32 percent since its $5.8 trillion peak in early October amid a broader AI sector pullback.
The decrease wiped out an astounding $550 billion in the week of the affair scandals, and a total of around $1.9 trillion since the October peak. Nvidia's market cap closed at $3.9 trillion on Friday.
Interim CEO Kress is now tasked with the daunting goal of steadying the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.
The Daily Mail has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s wife could land massive divorce settlement, attorney says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s wife could land massive divorce settlement, attorney says
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Jensen Huang lost his job, but not his stock. Soon, investors may not be able to see him sell it.
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board accepted Huang's resignation on Nov. 11. He walks away from about $108 million in unvested stock awards , pocket change next to the roughly 812 million shares he keeps, worth about $132 billion at Friday's close. That makes him Nvidia's largest individual owner.
When an insider sells, Wall Street sometimes reads it as a vote of no confidence in the company. When the founder of the world's most important AI chipmaker sells, the whole market can follow.
"This is no doubt an overhang on the trade for the foreseeable future," Liz Thomas, SoFi's chief market strategist, told Yahoo Finance on Thursday.
Investors are already voting. Nvidia stock closed Friday at its lowest level since July 2025, about 32% below its Oct. 6 record.
Legally, Huang can sell now. For three months after leaving, he still counts as a company insider, so any big sale needs a public notice filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission .
The legal cap on those sales won't slow him down. Based on trading before the scandal, it's about 600 million shares every three months, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's more than eight times the shares he holds in his own name.
But only his own shares are easy to sell, and the insider-trading rules don't expire in February.
The concern with hidden sales is that a former CEO might know bad news before the public does. Trading on that is still illegal, notice or no notice, and brokers keep records of every trade, which regulators can check.
About 70 million shares, worth about $11 billion, are in Huang's own name, according to his SEC filings . The other 740 million or so, worth about $121 billion, sit in family trusts, including one he runs with his wife, Lori. That setup makes a quick fire sale hard.
Even a full exit is smaller than it looks. His whole stake equals less than six days of typical Nvidia trading before the scandal, and Nvidia had $235 billion left on its buyback as of Sept. 28, enough to soak up every share he owns.
Nvidia typically reports fourth quarter results and files its annual report in late February. That leaves a gap of about two weeks after Huang's insider period ends, and that has drawn attention online.
Selling ahead of bad news he knew about would still be illegal.
Leaving doesn't erase his signature, either. Huang signed off on Nvidia's financial statements every quarter as CEO, and the quarter it reports Tuesday ended Oct. 25, on his watch.
That report will show whether Huang set up or canceled a preplanned trading plan before he left.
"If you're Jensen and you're just sort of this megastar all the time, you know, you stop thinking that rules apply to you," Bradley Tusk, co-founder of Tusk Venture Partners, told Yahoo Finance on Friday.

articles.content_orig:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCIV)  — More than 48 hours after the FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop, travelers at Charleston International Airport were still dealing with delays and cancellations.
Between 3:50 p.m. and 11:59 p.m., Sunday the airport’s website showed two canceled flights and more than 10 delays. Travelers said their departure times kept changing as they tried to get home.
Maureen Keenan and Kaleigh Macdonald came to Charleston from Boston for a wedding. They said their flight had been delayed repeatedly, shifting between hours.
The two said they were scared when they heard about the disruption. Some people they knew rented vans and left Saturday. If Keenan and Macdonald couldn’t fly out, they expected to stay in the Lowcountry.
Abby Terry’s birthday trip with 11 friends also took an unexpected turn. The group learned over dinner that most of their flights home had been canceled.
READ MORE | "Passengers scramble for alternatives as FAA ground stop snarled flights nationwide"
“We had very detailed plans, and I was like, ‘This was not on my itinerary, and ChatGPT did not tell me that this was going to happen,’” Terry said. “We were not prepared.”
Some of Terry’s friends began driving home. One left for an 18-hour trip back to Dallas, while others found a car and set out in a separate group.
Terry and several friends planned to take a shuttle to Atlanta and try to catch a flight. If that didn’t work, they expected to drive more than 10 hours home.
Travelers can check their flight status and TSA wait times on the airline or Charleston International Airport’s website.

articles.title_zh: China’s new home prices fall again in October; slowest annual decline in almost a year
articles.content_orig:
By Liangping Gao, Yukun Zhang and Ryan Woo
BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) – China’s new home prices declined again in October, albeit at the slowest annual rate in almost a year, extending a years-long slump that has eroded market confidence, sapped consumer spending ​and squeezed local government income.
Prices fell 0.1% versus September, when they also fell ‌0.1% on month, showed Reuters calculations based on data from the National Bureau of Statistics released on Monday.
They fell 2.4% versus October last year, the slowest pace of decline since November 2025. In September, prices fell 2.8% on year.
The data showed little indication of price recovery across the nation while conditions in big and small ‌cities ​continue to diverge, said analyst Zhang Dawei at Centaline Property. The ⁠number of cities with rising ⁠prices keeps shrinking, and signs of stabilisation are limited to a handful of areas, he said.
The sector, once an economic growth driver, has been the target of a slew of support measures yet has shown few signs of improvement. Analysts have said persistent price ​declines indicate the sector will likely remain a drag on the economy and that more drastic stimulus is needed.
A decline in property value shrinks homeowners’ wealth, nudging them to save instead ⁠of spend, especially amid a weak job market and ⁠slow wage growth.
Property investment, sales and new construction all continued to fall ​by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, official data showed.
For the sector ​to turn around, price stabilisation is necessary across cities, and property inventories need ‌to normalise, Lynn Song, ING chief economist for Greater China, wrote in a client note.
Smaller cities have experienced a prolonged downturn for both new and resale homes. Among the biggest cities, Shanghai alone registered both on-month and on-year price rises for both new and resale homes in October.
Resale ⁠home prices in so-called tier-one cities rose for an eighth month, indicating stability, though the trend is partly propelled by buyers opting for ready housing rather than risk waiting for projects that may ⁠not come to fruition, Zhang ‌said.
Completed homes that buyers can see and touch have become a kind ⁠of hard currency, and the “certainty premium” on resale homes is also ​showing, he ‌said.
To prop up consumer sentiment dampened by stalled housing projects, the ​government this ⁠year introduced measures to deter developers from selling homes before project completion.
Policymakers this year also introduced interest subsidies on new commercial mortgages for eligible first-time homebuyers.
Overall property investment and sales volume will likely keep falling for some time, and the sector will remain an economic drag next year, said equity analyst Jeff Zhang at Morningstar.
(Reporting by Liangping Gao, Yukun Zhang and Ryan Woo; Editing by Clarence ​Fernandez and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: Opinion | The New Congress Must Rein in Trump’s Dangerous China Policy
articles.title_zh: Opinion | The New Congress Must Rein in Trump’s Dangerous China Policy
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in Washington, DC, on Sept. 4, 2025.
Democrats and Republicans in the new Congress will disagree about plenty in health policy. However, they should agree that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) should be a scientific agency whose judgments hold steady no matter who occupies the White House. In January, Congress will have the chance to write that principle into law.
For decades, the scientific independence of America’s public health agencies rested on a bipartisan understanding. Presidential administrations disagreed about health policy, sometimes profoundly, but their health secretaries generally respected the expertise and established processes of agencies like the CDC and the Food and Drug Administration.
Earlier administrations of both parties—including those of Republican Secretary of Health and Human Services Alex Azar and Democratic Secretary Xavier Becerra —faced charges of political interference, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, and some had merit. But I would argue that none have even approached the scale and scope of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s interventions. The safeguards that existed were administrative policies, and a new secretary can discard them.
In June 2025, Kennedy dismissed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced them with his own appointees. No prior secretary had done this. Congress had given U.S. Health and Human Services secretaries broad authority and relied on their restraint. Restraint is a tradition, and the past year shows it can end.
To address this, Congress should pursue four priorities.
Elected leaders have a legitimate role in setting national health priorities and holding agencies accountable. That role ends where scientific judgment begins, and Congress should draw the line in statute:
Codify the advisory committee on immunization with clear membership qualifications, a transparent appointment process, and removal only for cause.
Require documented, public evidence reviews behind any major change to a scientific recommendation.
Require a secretary who departs from a formal recommendation to explain why in public, separating the scientific evidence from considerations like cost and implementation.
Protect career scientists’ ability to publish findings and communicate evidence, and create an independent office to investigate political interference, with whistleblower protections.
These rules must bind every future secretary, including those appointed by the party that controls Congress today. A protection that works against only one party’s appointees will not last.
The CDC has lost more than a quarter of its workforce since 2024. The losses include epidemiologists who investigate outbreaks, laboratory scientists who identify emerging pathogens, specialists who evaluate evidence, and professionals who work with state and local health departments. That expertise takes years to develop.
Congress should require an independent assessment of the CDC’s current capabilities and direct the agency to produce a public rebuilding plan with measurable targets for restoring essential functions. Personnel protections should support a professional scientific workforce that can serve administrations of either party. Targets should follow the agency’s mission, whatever headcount that implies.
COVID exposed confusion about the separate roles of the federal and state governments. The CDC could issue guidance, but implementation depended on state and local officials working under different laws, budgets, and political pressures.
Congress should specify what Americans can count on their national public health agency to do: investigate outbreaks when states request help, publish evidence-based guidance, and operate a national data system that state and local health departments can contribute to and draw from in near real time. It should fund those partners to participate, because the CDC’s guidance reaches Americans through their local health departments.
Scientific independence invites scrutiny, and protecting the CDC from political interference makes meaningful accountability more important. Congress should establish public measures of performance.
How effectively does the CDC identify and investigate emerging threats? How quickly does it get reliable information to states? How transparently does it evaluate evidence? How well does it communicate uncertainty and update recommendations as evidence changes?
An independent body should evaluate these questions, accounting for outcomes that depend on state and local partners. The purpose is to find weaknesses and improve performance.
With a Republican president in the White House, sweeping legislation will require bipartisan support. Congress can begin with oversight hearings, appropriations language, and independent investigations while it builds a coalition for lasting statutory protections. And they can start by pursuing common-sense, common-ground policies.
For eight decades , the CDC has protected Americans from infectious diseases and other health threats. Americans deserve a CDC whose science they can trust, whose expertise is protected, and whose ability to safeguard their health does not depend on who occupies the White House.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted efforts by other Trump administration officials to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China, sources tell Axios. Photo: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images
President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.
Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal.
Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen.
This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?"
Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic.
The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations.
Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.
Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for.
The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

articles.title_orig: Political setbacks at home complicate Trump’s China strategy
articles.title_zh: Political setbacks at home complicate Trump’s China strategy
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING/WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, reeling from a midterm election drubbing and Chinese spy allegations that have raised the stakes for his latest face-to-face with Beijing’s powerful leader, Xi Jinping.
Trump will first visit Manila for meetings with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders on Tuesday before jetting to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where he will meet the Chinese president and hold three-way discussions with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
With a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China extended to early next year, and more Trump-Xi talks due in December at the G20 in Miami, some analysts had initially billed the Shenzhen meeting as a low-stakes summit.
But a backlash against Trump’s Republican Party in this month’s midterms and criticism that his administration failed to act on intelligence that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, have muddied those expectations.
“With less reason to worry about market reactions or electoral fallout, (Trump) may be more willing to consider disruptive measures,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at the Tony Blair Institute, a London-based think tank.
Washington has already signalled such willingness ahead of the meeting, urging China to live up to its commitments made under the truce agreed between Trump and Xi a year ago.
Chinese analysts say they are particularly concerned that the Nvidia saga, including allegations that restricted semiconductors were diverted to Chinese customers, will now harden US attitudes towards China.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week there was growing consensus in Congress on further limiting Chinese access to advanced chips after the scandal, and Democrats are expected to press hard on the issue when they take over the House and Senate majorities in January.
China has said the United States has fabricated the spy narrative to justify a technological blockade.
Zhu Feng, director of the Institute of International Studies at Nanjing University, said the spat could also speed up “the decoupling of AI” between the world’s two superpowers even as they try to cooperate on mitigating the technology’s risks.
Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration said on condition of anonymity, adding that the Nvidia situation “should not really have any bearing on the trip.”
Rather than picking fresh fights with China, Trump may want to focus on legacy-building endeavours such as denuclearisation agreements with Beijing and Moscow, or securing another meeting with North Korea’s secretive leader, Kim Jong Un.
Trump sees the unprecedented summit with Xi and Putin as possibly providing movement towards an agreement on nuclear arms control. But that is a non-starter for China, which has far fewer warheads than the others, Chinese analysts said.
Trump may also seek to enlist Putin and Xi’s support in setting up a future meeting with Kim, who has close ties to the Chinese and Russian leaders.
The president will be focused on “building his legacy,” said Victor Cha at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank. A big part of that is his North Korea diplomacy, which he has devoted a lot of time to over his two terms, Cha added.
The proposed three-way meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
Such a framing is particularly worrisome for Ukraine, engaged in a four-year war with Russia. Trump is not expected to raise Ukraine at the meeting, the senior US official said.
Xi could also seek to take advantage of Trump’s political weakness after his election humbling, analysts say.
Top of Beijing’s wish list is ensuring that the US president doesn’t approve a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Trump has said he is holding the arms back as a “negotiating chip” with China.
But with China’s export engine humming, simply buying time may be enough for Beijing, said Jonathan Czin, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution, a US-based think tank.
“Xi just needs Trump to remain reluctant to revert toward a more competitive posture toward China for as long as possible. China will take whatever time it can get to fortify itself for the next round in the contest,” said Czin, who formerly worked at the Central Intelligence Agency and as director for China at the US National Security Council.
Beijing will be acutely aware that whoever succeeds Trump when his term ends in two years time, may be less accommodating, said Czin and Osman.
Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, repeatedly angered China with comments over human rights issues and a pledge that the US would defend Taiwan if Beijing attacked. Many of Trump’s potential Republican successors, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are also seen as more hawkish on China.
Both leaders will also be wary of reigniting a trade row that threatened to tank the global economy and financial markets last year, said Kurt Tong, a former senior State Department official now with the Asia Group think tank.
Despite the frustration the US has voiced on Chinese implementation of the terms of the truce, Tong expects it will be further extended beyond its January 10 expiration.
“The two sides are quite incentivized to maintain this fragile stability … despite also having some disagreements,” added senior China analyst Chim Lee at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
“They both have quite a lot to lose.”

What I Cover
Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…
Oil prices began the week with a further loss amid reports that the global oil market is returning to oversupply, even as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue and Iraq is forced to export crude by truck via Syria.
Brent crude was trading at $95.24 per barrel at the time of writing, and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $88.31 per barrel, both slightly down from Friday’s close.
The dip followed a report from the International Energy Agency saying that the oil market will swing back into oversupply during the current quarter. The agency cited lower demand, resulting from the higher prices, and the recovery of supply in the Middle East.
Notably, however, the IEA also said that on an annual basis, global oil supply would be 4.8 million barrels daily lower than in 2025, while demand would only decline by 2.7 million barrels daily.
Apparently, traders did not focus on this bit of information, likely because the IEA report was not the only one predicting a return to the glut. Earlier this month, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan analysts both issued predictions of a glut, citing the demand destruction caused by the war between the United States and Israel and Iran.
“We estimate the global oil market returned to a surplus of 1.1 million barrels per day ‌in September, widening to 1.4 million bpd in October, nearly matching last year's average of 1.3 million bpd,” JP Morgan said, while Goldman estimated a balanced oil market for September and October, being more guarded with the glut predictions.
“For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness. That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone,” KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters.
ING commodity analysts, meanwhile, noted that risks remain. “Regional crude flows are approaching pre-war levels, but exports continue to rely on alternative routes around the Strait of Hormuz, leaving supply vulnerable to further disruption,” they wrote in a note at the end of last week.
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.title_zh: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.content_orig:
It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up.
Ever since 1982, when Ronald Reagan traded a recession, 11% unemployment and Democrats’ 26-seat pickup for a five-day swing through Latin America, Air Force One has been leaving political upheaval behind in its contrail.
President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his authoritarian counterparts from China and Russia — a splashy show of geopolitical theater alongside men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchallenged.
Comparisons with a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable.
The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status. He’ll be joined on the trip by Elon Musk, whose $445 million in political spending failed to deliver Republican majorities.
“Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.”
It’s not the only complication on Trump’s plate. The scandal involving Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips and affair with an alleged Chinese spy will loom over the US president’s visit to Shenzhen, the gleaming hub of China’s tech industry, even though Trump’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey.
Trump doesn’t intend to raise the spying matter with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, American officials have previously told CNN. Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to further restrict high-powered chips from going to China .
“It’s probably not something we’re going to read the Chinese in on at the moment,” one senior US official said.
Never particularly enthusiastic about grueling trips through far-flung time zones, Trump departs for the Philippines Monday after shaking up his West Wing leadership and facing calls even from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense. An air travel meltdown before he left — which Trump did not address publicly for days — also raised new questions about his mindset and focus heading into the trip.
At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in a region that for decades has suffered from Washington’s inattention.
Like his most recent predecessors, Trump has found the “pivot to Asia” an elusive concept. His second term became bogged down by a war in the Middle East, the same region that kept George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden from fully turning American foreign policy toward the Pacific.
Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said.
Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s so-far futile efforts to end the war in Ukraine , continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks this week in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts.
So, too, will Democrats’ stateside victories lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters.
A foreign trip has long been a way to drive home that point while also escaping Washington as the opposition prepares to assume power. Michael Deaver, an image-maker to Reagan, is credited with inventing the tactic when he arranged the Latin America trip in 1982.
Nearly every president since then has replicated the idea. Bill Clinton made a trip to the Philippines in November 1994 after Republicans swept control of Congress for the first time in decades. George W. Bush was in Vietnam a few weeks after the GOP lost Congress in 2006. Barack Obama headed to Asia in 2010 and 2014 after midterm routs. And Trump himself made a somewhat desultory visit to France in 2017 after the GOP lost its majority in the House.
“I’ve been with presidents immediately after midterm, both wins and losses, and it’s always important,” Kagan said. “It’s something that reminds the nation, it reminds foreign observers, that this is very much the president’s bailiwick.”
For Trump, that means appearing in a joint setting with powerful men to discuss the world’s affairs. For some, the meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin carries unpleasant echoes of the 1945 conference in the Crimean resort of Yalta, where Stalin, Churchill and an extremely ill Franklin D. Roosevelt carved up the postwar world into western and eastern spheres of influence.
Putin originally proposed the three-party summit as a venue to discuss the Ukraine war, where fraught issues of borders and sovereignty loom over nascent peace talks.
Trump’s aides insist Thursday’s meeting is nothing of the sort, and say Ukraine won’t even be on the agenda. Instead, Trump hopes to open discussions on nuclear weapons with two leaders he’s worked hard to cultivate. The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia — which each have an estimated 5,000 warheads — expired in February. China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its arsenal to more than 600 warheads but shows little interest in joining a pact.
China’s ‘miracle city’ that no US president has visited (yet)
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said expectations were low for a major breakthrough, describing the talks instead as a starting point.
“It’s time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said.
Xi had initially appeared skeptical of hosting the meeting, officials said, concerned it could overshadow the APEC summit and his attempts to showcase a rising China. But on Monday China’s foreign ministry billed it as meeting of “groundbreaking significance,” with spokesperson Mao Ning saying “such efforts would will help stabilize the global situation.”
Trump, who sometimes says he envies authoritarians who rule as they wish, signed on quickly.

articles.content_orig:

A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. Photo: Reuters
Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair.
Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race.
Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer.
Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below.
Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance.
Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms.
Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips.
In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata . Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company.
Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning.
By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg , and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP .
Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline.
More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times .
State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated  export-control restrictions.
What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Jensen Huang on Nov. 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign threats.

articles.title_orig: Bitcoin’s Fall to $62,000 Sparks Market Manipulation Claims
articles.title_zh: Bitcoin’s Fall to $62,000 Sparks Market Manipulation Claims
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Michael Van De Poppe said it was still the middle of the correction and market acceleration.
Over the weekend, Strategy's Michael Saylor hinted at another buying opportunity.
The rebound came after a sharp slide, as Bitcoin and Ethereum hit multi-month lows.
Bitcoin (BTC) recovered on Sunday after falling to about $62,100 a day earlier, which Crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe said could turn into a "mean-reversion play," but warned the market has not bottomed.
Van de Poppe, founder of MN Fund, said on X that the drop had been severe. "After such a massive crash (and we don't know where the bottom is), it's possible to be seeing a mean-reversion play," he wrote. A mean-reversion move happens when a price snaps back toward its average after a sharp swing.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
Van de Poppe said that it "could be to $70-72K" for Bitcoin. For Ethereum (ETH), he put the range at $2,050 to $2,100.
He was clear that a rebound would not mark the end of the sell-off. "That doesn't mean we're bottoming out at all; it's still the middle of the correction and acceleration in the markets," he said. Still, he saw value in the swings. "High volatility = high chances of opportunity = also great for long-term investments," he wrote.
On Stocktwits, Bitcoin was one of the top trending tickers among cryptocurrencies at the time of writing. Bitcoin's price was trading near $64,800 on Sunday, up over 2% in 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC moved to 'neutral' from 'extremely bearish,' zones, as chatter around it stayed at high levels over the past day.
Ethereum's price also recovered, up over 4% on Sunday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ETH moved to 'bullish' from 'bearish' zones, as chatter around it stayed at 'high' levels over the past day.
CoinGlass data showed $386.64 million worth of positions were liquidated across the market in 24 hours, wiping out 76,220 traders. Short sellers accounted for almost 69% of the $265.67 million in losses. Bitcoin led the flush with $200 million in liquidations, mostly shorts. The biggest single hit was a $8.92 million short on Bitcoin on Hyperliquid (HYPE) at $65,539. Ether came in second with $94.24 million liquidated. Most of the $16.47 million liquidated in the past hour was in long positions, suggesting prices are cooling off.
Bitcoin's biggest corporate holders, meanwhile, signaled they were ready to buy the dip. Strategy (MSTR) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor posted a chart of the company's purchases, saying "This dip could use a little orange." The chart showed Strategy holding about 850,360 Bitcoin at an average cost of about $75,450. At current prices, those holdings were down 13.5%.
Strive (ASST) CEO Matt Cole shared a similar chart of his company's roughly 43,150 Bitcoin. "Bitcoin's cheap, we want more," he wrote.
Prices rebounded after a sharp slide, with Bitcoin falling below $66,000 on Saturday for the first time since August and Ethereum touching a low of about $1,713, its weakest level since July .

articles.title_orig: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.title_zh: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title_orig: ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
articles.title_zh: ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
articles.content_orig:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have failed to conclude long-running negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea during meetings in Manila, despite tentative agreement on about 80 percent of a draft, the Philippines’ foreign minister said.
“There is no conclusion yet,” Theresa Lazaro told reporters at the ASEAN summit on Sunday, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.
“The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added.
ASEAN and Beijing have been working on a code ⁠of conduct in the South China Sea, where they have overlapping claims, for more than two decades. The Philippines, as the current chair of the 11-nation association, had pledged to speed up the process and reach a deal by the end of this year.
Lazaro said she still hoped the code could be concluded under Singapore’s auspices, as the city-state takes over as chair next year.
Southeast Asian nations want the code to reflect international law, which some of them accuse China of ignoring. Beijing insists its actions have been lawful and professional.
China has laid claim to most of the South China Sea, clashing with the exclusive economic zones ⁠of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, making a functional code essential to keeping tensions from escalating and managing maritime encounters.
An international arbitration tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
China and the Philippines, in particular, have faced off in a series of maritime confrontations in recent years.
The Philippines accuses Chinese ships of repeated ⁠aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, firing water cannons and ⁠disrupting resupply missions. China accuses the Philippines of intruding on its territory.
Tensions escalated after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. Months of harsh words between the two countries over the sea preceded this weekend’s meetings.
Separately, ASEAN extended a ban on Myanmar’s leader attending the bloc’s annual summits, saying the country failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan.
ASEAN leaders also decried Myanmar’s military and armed groups for continuing to attack civilians in the country’s long-running civil war.
Under the ban, Myanmar can be represented only by lower-level career diplomats, including at the summit in Manila. Myanmar was due to hold ASEAN’s rotating chair this year, but because of the civil strife, the role passed to the Philippines.
The stern rebuke followed a review of progress on the Five-Point Consensus for Myanmar, approved by ASEAN in April 2021 in a bid to ease the violence that erupted after Myanmar’s military seized power from the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February that year.
The military coup triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.
In Manila, ASEAN leaders expressed “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the plan and urged all parties to “stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
There are “still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people, so step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we’ll monitor that,” said Lazaro, who is also ASEAN’s current special envoy to Myanmar.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, the former chief of the military, has made official visits to several ASEAN member states since assuming the presidency after elections in December and January, widely seen as having been rigged.
ASEAN has not discouraged those visits, but its leaders have emphasised that the peace plan remains “the main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar”.

articles.title_orig: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.title_zh: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.content_orig:
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.
The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.
The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.
Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.
Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”
The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week .

articles.title_orig: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.title_zh: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 8,800 flights were delayed and 2,400 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

articles.title_orig: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
articles.title_zh: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
articles.content_orig:
Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.
A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.
Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.
The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.
“The Houthis are very determined to go to Aden,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “They don’t want to see any area controlled by the government or the Saudi side, so they want to take over everything at this moment.”

articles.title_orig: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.title_zh: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.
Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

articles.content_orig:
Update [ Sun 15th Nov 2026, 7:17pm ]:
It's official! These animations are now rolling out to all players on Xbox One, Series X and Series S:
Original Story: So, you remember that recent Xbox console update we mentioned yesterday ? The one that happened on Wednesday and included original Xbox achievements ? It seems like there's at least one more hidden feature to be discovered.
A couple of eagle-eyed Xbox fans have spotted that the patch notes had been adjusted for this update last night, and they mentioned that three classic startup animations were being added to "celebrate 25 years of Xbox history".
The three animations are for the original Xbox, Xbox 360 (2005) and Xbox 360 (2010).
Since then, the patch notes have been adjusted once more to just reference "miscellaneous" improvements, so it seems like they jumped the gun slightly and were supposed to wait until November 15th (the date of Xbox's 25th anniversary ) to reveal these three startup animations.
None of them are live yet by the way, but it might be worth checking the "Startup" section of your Xbox console's Settings menu periodically over the next couple of days to see if they show up.
I don't know about you, but I'm going to be rocking the original Xbox startup animation as soon as possible!

articles.title_zh: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
articles.content_orig:
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Houthis claim missile attack on Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: Houthis claim missile attack on Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognized Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el Mandeb strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government’s retreat ​from the Bab el Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime choke point, creating ‌a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el Mandeb strait is one ​of the world’s most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly ​from Asia to Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were ⁠redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, ​including the capital Sanaa and Yemen’s most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
“The Southern ​Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the southern forces said in a statement.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the ​capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.”
Government ​forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south ‌in September ⁠in an attempt to seize control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ​ally and the world’s biggest ​crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on ⁠the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the 9-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ​ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom’s Red Sea oil ​export hub ⁠of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting ⁠is intensifying ​around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The ​city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to ​enter, and civilians are unable to leave.
